query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying stationary friction processing (SFP) to equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy improves its resistance to oxidation compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with coarse grains (~98 μm) that tend to form nonprotective spinel oxides during oxidation.
generation.intervention: Stationary friction processing using a tungsten carbide (WC) cylindrical tool at high rotational speeds (e.g., 1800 rpm for 5 minutes).
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at elevated temperatures (850 °C, 950 °C, and 1050 °C) for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction of grain size from coarse (~98 μm) to ultrafine grains (down to ~0.43 μm) with increased grain boundary density.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine-grain microstructure promotes rapid Cr diffusion via abundant grain boundaries, which enables the formation of a dense and protective Cr2O3 (and subsequently Al2O3) oxide layer, while the increased surface free energy reduces the formation of nonprotective spinel oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant deceleration in oxidation kinetics as evidenced by reduced mass gain and lower parabolic rate constants relative to the as-cast alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast high-entropy alloy exhibiting slower diffusion paths, formation of nonprotective oxides, and higher oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys processed by SFP under the specified conditions. Variations in alloy composition or processing parameters might lead to different outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of oxidation resistance improvement and potential impacts of secondary phase transformations remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy samples: one set in the as-cast state and one set processed by SFP at 1800 rpm. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850 °C, 950 °C, and 1050 °C, each for a duration of 100 hours.
measurements: Grain size and microstructural characterization via microscopy
Mass gain measurements over time to determine oxidation kinetics
Phase analysis (e.g., XRD) to identify the type and distribution of oxides formed
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SFP-processed samples do not display statistically significant lower mass gains, slower oxidation kinetics (lower parabolic rate constants), or formation of predominantly protective Cr2O3/Al2O3 layers compared to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h. Findings: Grain size refined from 98 μm (as-cast) to 1 μm (SFP_400) and 0.43 μm (SFP_1800).; Phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC occurred, with 38% and 55% FCC fraction for SFP_400 and SFP_1800, respectively.; Surface free energy increased by 29.8% for SFP_400 and 35.2% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Oxidation kinetics decelerated by 12–20% for SFP_400 and 38–48% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Cumulative mass gain at 850 °C after 100 h was 0.33 mg/cm² (as-cast), 0.27 mg/cm² (SFP_400), and 0.17 mg/cm² (SFP_1800).; Parabolic rate constants (k_p) at 1050 °C were 23.2 × 10⁻¹³ g²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹ (as-cast), 18.4 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_400), and 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_1800).; Processed samples formed predominantly protective
